write.desc: The mean value theorem family (Fermat, Rolle, Lagrange and Cauchy) and what follows from it: constancy, monotonicity, Lipschitz bounds, inequalities, root counting and Darboux's theorem. These points belong together because each consequence is proved by choosing a function and an interval and applying one of these few theorems, whose exact hypotheses must be checked every time.

points.name: Local extrema and Fermat's theorem
points.what: The learner can define local maxima and minima and prove that if a function has a local extremum at an interior point where it is differentiable, then the derivative there is zero. They can explain why endpoints and points of non-differentiability must be checked separately (|x| at 0, x on [0,1]), why f'(c) = 0 does not force an extremum (x^3), and how to find the extreme values of a continuous function on a closed interval.
outside: definition of the derivative as a limit of difference quotients, including one-sided limits
limits preserve non-strict inequalities (order limit theorem for functions)

points.name: Rolle's theorem
points.what: The learner can state and prove Rolle's theorem (f continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), f(a) = f(b) gives some c in (a, b) with f'(c) = 0) by combining the extreme value theorem with Fermat's theorem, and can show with counterexamples that each hypothesis is needed.
outside: extreme value theorem: a continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains its maximum and minimum

points.name: The mean value theorem
points.what: The learner can state the mean value theorem with its exact hypotheses (continuity on the closed interval, differentiability on the open one), prove it from Rolle's theorem by subtracting the secant line, read it geometrically as a tangent parallel to the chord, and understand that c is only known to exist somewhere in (a, b).

points.name: The Cauchy mean value theorem
points.what: The learner can state and prove the generalised mean value theorem (f(b) - f(a))g'(c) = (g(b) - g(a))f'(c) by applying Rolle's theorem to a suitable combination of f and g, explain why applying the ordinary mean value theorem to f and g separately fails (it gives two different points), and interpret it as the mean value theorem for a parametric curve.

points.name: Zero derivative means constant
points.what: The learner can prove that a function with zero derivative on an interval is constant, and hence that two functions with equal derivatives on an interval differ by a constant, and can show the result fails on a set that is not an interval (for example a function equal to 0 on (0, 1) and 1 on (2, 3)).

points.name: The sign of the derivative and monotonicity
points.what: The learner can prove that on an interval f' >= 0 everywhere holds exactly when f is increasing, that f' > 0 everywhere makes f strictly increasing, and that the converse of the strict version fails (x^3 at 0). They can use this to find the intervals where a function increases or decreases.

points.name: What a positive derivative at a single point does and does not give
points.what: The learner can prove from the definition that f'(c) > 0 gives f(x) > f(c) for x slightly to the right of c and f(x) < f(c) slightly to the left, and can show with x + 2x^2 sin(1/x) at 0 that f still need not be increasing on any interval around c, so a pointwise sign condition is weaker than a sign condition on an interval.
outside: definition of the derivative as a limit of difference quotients
the example x^2 sin(1/x), differentiable everywhere with derivative not continuous at 0

points.name: Bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz bound
points.what: The learner can prove that |f'| <= M on an interval implies |f(x) - f(y)| <= M|x - y|, conclude that f is uniformly continuous there, and apply it to examples such as |sin x - sin y| <= |x - y| and sqrt x on [1, infinity). They also see the converse direction: a differentiable Lipschitz function has a bounded derivative.
outside: Lipschitz functions and uniform continuity, and that Lipschitz implies uniformly continuous

points.name: Proving inequalities with the mean value theorem
points.what: The learner can prove inequalities such as sin x <= x for x >= 0, e^x >= 1 + x, ln(1 + x) <= x and Bernoulli's inequality (1 + x)^r >= 1 + rx for r >= 1 and x > -1, either by applying the mean value theorem on a well-chosen interval or by showing an auxiliary difference function is monotone and checking its value at one point. They can also derive two-sided estimates such as 1/(2 sqrt(n + 1)) < sqrt(n + 1) - sqrt(n) < 1/(2 sqrt(n)).
outside: familiar derivatives of sin, cos, exp, log and power functions, used as known

points.name: Counting and locating roots with Rolle's theorem
points.what: The learner can use Rolle's theorem to show that between two zeros of f lies a zero of f', so that if f' never vanishes then f has at most one root, and combine this with the intermediate value theorem to prove an equation such as x^5 + x - 1 = 0 has exactly one real root. They can bound the number of roots of a function by the number of roots of its derivative plus one (for example, a polynomial of degree n has at most n real roots, by induction).
outside: intermediate value theorem for continuous functions

points.name: The limit of the derivative and one-sided derivatives
points.what: The learner can prove with the mean value theorem that if f is continuous at c, differentiable near c, and f'(x) tends to L as x tends to c, then f is differentiable at c with f'(c) = L (and the one-sided version). They can use this to check differentiability of piecewise-defined functions at the joining point, and see from x^2 sin(1/x) that the derivative can exist at c even when the limit of f'(x) does not.
outside: the example x^2 sin(1/x), differentiable everywhere with derivative not continuous at 0

points.name: Darboux's theorem: derivatives have the intermediate value property
points.what: The learner can prove that if f is differentiable on [a, b] and lambda lies strictly between f'(a) and f'(b), then f'(c) = lambda for some c in (a, b), by finding an interior minimum or maximum of f(x) - lambda x and applying Fermat's theorem. They conclude that a derivative cannot have a jump discontinuity (so a step function is not a derivative), even though, as x^2 sin(1/x) shows, a derivative need not be continuous.
outside: extreme value theorem: a continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains its maximum and minimum
the example x^2 sin(1/x), differentiable everywhere with derivative not continuous at 0
jump discontinuities and the classification of discontinuities
